title: SAGE: Evidence-First Biomarker Discovery through Multi-Agent Reasoning
claim: A chain of specialized agents, supported by a knowledge graph and validation tools, turns a question into an evidence-grounded, validated hypothesis.
layout: 3 panels: wide top agent chain, bottom-left graph pipeline, bottom-right tools; feedback loop
description: A three-panel system diagram. Panel A, spanning the top, is a snake-like flow of colored role boxes, each with a cartoon agent icon. It runs from Human User and prompt through Path Generation, Ontologist, Scientist, Hypothesis Expansion and Human Feedback. A red loop connects Feedback and Novelty Debate Agent back to the Scientist. It then runs right to left on the second row through Explainability, Validation, Results Interpreter and Summary Agent, ending at a document stack. PubMed and Semantic Scholar logos sit under the debate agent. Panel B, bottom left, is a knowledge-graph pipeline: papers and textbooks, text chunking, triple extraction, blacklist filtering, local graph, node fusion and global graph. Panel C, bottom right, shows an MCP Orchestrator connected to tool suites, a Coding Agent and a Dataset Discovery Agent, with data sources below. Pastel fills and thick black panel borders organize the layout.
caption: Overview of the SAGE framework for computational pathology. The pipeline comprises three stages: (A) Hypothesis generation and refinement (top), where coordinated agents produce interpretable hypotheses with optional human feedback at key decision points; (B) Knowledge graph construction and reasoning (bottom left), integrating pathology-aware biomedical entities to support structured biological reasoning; and (C) Validation and summarization (bottom right), which executes statistical analyses and generates clinically interpretable summaries.
abstract: Engineered image-based biomarkers offer a clinically interpretable alternative to black-box AI in computational pathology, yet their discovery remains largely intuition-driven, guided by fragmented literature rather than rigorous biological validation. We introduce SAGE (Structured Agentic system for hypothesis Generation and Evaluation), a multi-agent framework that grounds biomarker discovery in biological evidence through three mechanisms: (i) knowledge-graph-anchored hypothesis generation via multi-path ontological reasoning, (ii) a debate-based multi-agent novelty assessment that stress-tests candidate biomarkers against existing literature, and (iii) an end-to-end automated validation pipeline that translates hypotheses directly into executable analyses on multimodal pathology datasets. Together, these components shift biomarker discovery from an intuition-driven, literature-browsing exercise into a structured, traceable reasoning process that clinicians and researchers can inspect, trust, and build upon.
